title: Krishna's Morning in Dvaraka
hook: the queens curse the roosters for crowing. Krishna gets up and keeps an ordinary morning, on purpose
carry: the ordinary morning is part of dharma
tomorrow: a sage wakes two princes in the dark. what is waiting?

segments.voice: Yesterday, Arjuna's mind like the wind, and Krishna's answer: evenness is yoga, and the doshas' evenness is health.

Dvaraka, before dawn. In the Bhagavata Purana the roosters start crowing, and Krishna's queens curse them, because the crowing means he's about to leave their side. The roosters don't care. Krishna gets up. And then the text does something you might not expect in a story about God. It walks through his morning, step by step. He touches water. He sits in silent meditation. He bathes, puts on clean clothes, and does his morning prayers and offerings, repeating a sacred mantra in silence, before he sees anyone at all.
screen: `THE ROOSTERS CROW.` → `THE QUEENS CURSE THEM.` → `KRISHNA GETS UP.`

segments.voice: Then he greets the rising sun, honors his elders, gives gifts, and only after that turns to the business of the day. Why spend all those words on God's morning? One answer comes from Krishna himself, in the Gita: whatever the great do, others follow. If I didn't keep to my work, people everywhere would follow my lead. So the Lord keeps an ordinary morning, on purpose. That's the teaching: in Hindu life the ordinary morning is part of dharma, not the boring part before it. Many homes still keep its shape: a bath before worship, clean clothes, then the lamp and a prayer. The Yoga Sutra names cleanness, shaucha, first among the observances it asks for. Ayurveda gives the same morning its own name: dinacharya. Dina, day; charya, conduct; the day's conduct. The Charaka Samhita's chapter on daily regimen starts with eating in the right measure, then walks through things anyone would recognize: caring for the eyes, cleaning the teeth with a twig, scraping the tongue, rinsing the mouth, oil for the body, a bath, clean clothes. One text calls this health; the other calls it dharma. They keep the same hours. And today? It's easy to treat the morning as something to get through before life starts. Krishna's story says the morning is where the day is first offered. The toothbrush counts. The shower before the prayer counts.
screen: `WHAT THE GREAT DO, OTHERS FOLLOW.` · `THE MORNING IS PART OF DHARMA.` · `DINACHARYA: THE DAY'S CONDUCT.` · `ONE MORNING: HEALTH AND DHARMA.`

segments.voice: Picture tomorrow morning, step by step: water, the sink, the shower, clean clothes. If you pray, choose one of those ordinary acts and offer it to God before you do it, the way a bath comes before puja. If you don't pray, choose one and decide now to do it slowly and on purpose, the way the Bhagavata walks through Krishna's.
The daily routine. Dinacharya, the day's conduct: the morning round of the Ayurvedic texts, kept in Hindu homes beside the bath, the lamp and the first prayer.
Your line: the ordinary morning is part of dharma. Even Krishna kept one. Rest well.

howItsDone: Many Hindus bathe and put on clean clothes before the morning puja, then light a lamp and pray; Ayurveda's dinacharya (cleaning the teeth, scraping the tongue, oil, bath) runs alongside, and the Bhagavata's account of Krishna's morning in Dvaraka is one picture of that ordinary, sacred round.
